c.tagline: Poland's western cradle — where clockwork goats butt heads and a croissant crowns a saint.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; booking through an app (Bolt, Free Now or iTaxi) is usually cheaper and easier than a street hail.

emergency.note: 112 is the pan-European emergency number reaching police, fire and ambulance; operators generally speak English.

hood_landmark.Stare Miasto (Old Market Square): Poznań Old Market Square Stary Rynek

avoid.reason: Late-night rowdiness around Stary Rynek bars and occasional pickpockets at the main train station deserve normal awareness.

hood_desc: The Renaissance core around the Old Market Square (Stary Rynek), famed for its colourful merchant houses, the ornate Town Hall whose mechanical goats butt heads at noon, and a ring of restaurants and bars; the natural walkable base for first-timers.

Poznań's trendiest district just northwest of the centre, a grid of restored tenements packed with independent cafes, bistros, bars and the lively Rynek Jeżycki market; best for a hip, local, going-out crowd.

A dignified residential district south of the centre around the Łazarz market hall and the historic Poznań International Fair grounds (MTP), with wide streets and Art Nouveau tenements; a calm base close to the action.
A regenerated former working-class district anchored by the vast Stary Browar arts-and-shopping centre in a converted brewery, with parks and a growing café scene; up-and-coming and good value.

The green eastern reach of the city built around Lake Malta, with its regatta course, year-round ski slope, thermal baths and Nowe Zoo; best for families and travellers wanting recreation and open water.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some locals prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: Tickets run on time (from a short 15-minute ticket) rather than distance; buy them from onboard machines, kiosks, or the jakdojade/mPay/moBILET apps and validate on boarding. Contactless bank cards can be tapped on many vehicles. A short-time ticket costs about 4 PLN (~$1.10) and a 24-hour ticket about 15 PLN (~$4).
transit.hours: Trams and buses run about 5am–11pm, after which night lines take over across the city.

bus: Poznań Główny Bus Station (PKS, at the main railway station)

transit.m: MPK bus 159 to Poznań Główny railway station, ~25 min
MPK bus 222 to Rondo Kaponiera / centre, ~20 min

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving about 10% for good service in restaurants is appreciated. State the total you want to pay when handing over money, as simply saying 'thank you' can be taken to mean 'keep the change'.

food.name: Rogal swietomarcinski (St Martin's croissant)
food.desc: Poznan's EU-protected croissant: flaky puff pastry coiled around white poppy seed, nuts and candied orange, iced and sprinkled.

places.name: Rogalowe Muzeum Poznania
places.note: Old Market Square museum where you watch the croissant made, then eat a warm one.

places.name: Cukiernia Kandulski
places.note: Long-running family patisserie locals rate as the benchmark for the certified rogal.

places.name: Rynek Jezycki bakery stalls
places.note: Neighbourhood market where certified bakers sell them by weight, cheaper than the tourist core.

food.name: Pyry z gzikiem
food.desc: The Poznan comfort plate: hot jacket potatoes with cold twarog quark whipped with soured cream, chives, radish and onion.

places.name: Pyra Bar
places.note: Whole menu built around potatoes; the standard address for a cheap, correct plate of pyry z gzikiem.

places.name: Gospoda Pod Koziolkami
places.note: Old-style Wielkopolska inn on the main square doing the regional classics.

places.name: Ratuszova
places.note: Cellar restaurant under the town hall with a dedicated old-Poznan section on the menu.

food.name: Plendze (Poznan potato pancakes)
food.desc: Thin, lacy grated-potato pancakes fried crisp; eaten savoury with sour cream and mushroom sauce or sweet with sugar.

places.name: Pyra Bar
places.note: Several versions on one menu, including the goulash-topped plendze.

places.name: Gospoda Pod Koziolkami
places.note: Fried to order in a traditional tavern setting.

places.name: Bar mleczny Apetyt
places.note: Milk-bar prices for a very local, very filling plate.

food.name: Czernina
food.desc: Wielkopolska's famous sweet-sour duck blood soup, darkened with blood and vinegar, sweetened with dried fruit and served over noodles.

places.name: Ratuszova
places.note: Keeps the old regional soups on the card year-round.

places.name: Gospoda Pod Koziolkami
places.note: Traditional inn that cooks czernina the old Wielkopolska way.

places.name: Bamberka
places.note: Named for Poznan's Bamberg settlers and built around historic local recipes.

food.name: Kaczka po poznansku
food.desc: Roast duck Poznan-style, served with braised red cabbage and pyzy - soft steamed yeast dumplings that soak up the juices.

places.name: Bamberka
places.note: Heritage-recipe restaurant on the square; duck is its signature main.

places.name: Ratuszova
places.note: Reliable full-size portion of the city's benchmark roast.

places.name: Brovaria
places.note: Brewpub-hotel restaurant pairing the duck with its own house lager.

food.name: Szagowki and parzybroda
food.desc: Deep-cut Wielkopolska cooking: diamond-cut potato dumplings with bacon, and parzybroda, a soupy cabbage-and-potato stew.

places.name: Pyra Bar
places.note: Best chance of finding the rarer potato dishes on a printed menu.

places.name: Gospoda Pod Koziolkami
places.note: Rotates old country dishes through its daily specials.

food.name: Poznan beer
food.desc: The city gave Poland the Lech brand, but the fun now is in Wielkopolska craft brewers pouring in Old Town multitaps.

places.name: Brovaria
places.note: Brews unfiltered lager and wheat beer in-house right on the Old Market Square.

places.name: Piwna Stopa
places.note: Long-running multitap with a rotating wall of Polish craft taps.

places.name: Stary Browar surrounds
places.note: Old brewery complex turned mall, ringed by bars for a post-shopping pint.

food.name: Miod pitny and nalewki
food.desc: Polish mead in graded strengths plus nalewki - homemade fruit and herb infusions poured as a digestif after a heavy Wielkopolska meal.

places.name: Bamberka
places.note: Serves mead and house infusions alongside the heritage food menu.

places.name: Gospoda Pod Koziolkami
places.note: Tavern list of meads and flavoured vodkas by the glass.

places.name: Ratuszova

landmarks: Stary Rynek (Old Market Square)
Ringed by candy-colored merchant houses lovingly rebuilt after wartime ruin, Poznan's Renaissance square ranks among Europe's most beautiful marketplaces.
Town Hall and the Fighting Goats
At noon crowds crane below the Renaissance town hall clock as two mechanical billy goats emerge to butt heads twelve times.
Ostrow Tumski (Cathedral Island)
Poland's oldest cathedral island holds the Gothic basilica where the nation's first rulers, Mieszko I and Boleslaw the Brave, lie buried.
Imperial Castle (Zamek)
Built for Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1910, this hulking neo-Romanesque castle now thrives as a cultural center with cinema, galleries and cafes.
Fara Poznanska (Parish Church of St. Stanislaus)
One of Poland's grandest baroque churches overwhelms with rose-marble columns, gilded stucco and free summer recitals on its famous organ.
Porta Posnania
A sleek concrete-and-glass multimedia museum across the river interprets a thousand years of Polish history born on Cathedral Island.
Rogalowe Muzeum (Croissant Museum)
Live baking shows in a Renaissance tenement reveal how Poznan's crescent St. Martin croissants earned protected status, with generous tastings included.
Citadel Park (Cytadela)
The hilltop remains of a vast Prussian fortress now hold war cemeteries, military museums and Magdalena Abakanowicz's haunting Unrecognized sculpture crowd.
Stary Browar
A former brewery reborn as an award-winning art-and-shopping center, its soaring brick atriums blend contemporary sculpture with designer boutiques.
Lake Malta
This rowing-regatta lake east of the center offers a year-round toboggan run, ski slope, thermal baths complex and lakeside promenades.

train.note: Poznań sits on the main Warsaw-Berlin line, so it has the best direct German connection in Poland - Berlin Hauptbahnhof is about three hours away on the Berlin-Warszawa-Express, running several times a day. Warsaw takes 2h30 by Pendolino and Wrocław 2. Poznań Główny is west of the old town. Book on the Intercity site for the cheaper advance fares.

bus.note: Coaches use the terminal at Poznań Główny. FlixBus runs to Berlin in about 4 hours and across Germany and the Netherlands, serving the large Polish diaspora - the train is faster to Berlin but the coach is cheaper. Carry your passport or EU ID card.

ferry.note: Poznań is inland on the Warta river, which carries no scheduled passenger service, so there are no ferries. Poland's Baltic crossings leave from Gdynia, Świnoujście and Gdańsk.

half.name: Rogalin & Kórnik
half.blurb: A pair of aristocratic estates south of Poznań — the Baroque Rogalin Palace with its ancient oaks and the neo-Gothic Kórnik Castle and arboretum.

half.name: Gniezno
half.blurb: Poland's first capital and the cradle of the Polish state, with a Gothic cathedral holding the bronze Gniezno Doors, about an hour away.

full.name: Toruń
full.blurb: The UNESCO-listed Gothic birthplace of Copernicus, famed for its gingerbread and riverside old town, about two hours from Poznań.

full.name: Biskupin
full.blurb: A reconstructed Iron Age fortified settlement on a lake, one of Poland's most important archaeological sites.
